passages.title: The Tall Tower
sentences: Sam, Ana and Ben played a block game at a table.
They stacked blocks to make a tower.
The tower got very tall.
Then Pixel ran under the table to get his ball.
His tail hit a table leg, and the table shook.
The tower fell down.
Everyone laughed.
Then they started a new game.

passages.title: The Muddy Field
sentences: On a Saturday in April, Ana had a soccer match.
She put on her red shirt and her soccer shoes.
Then it started to rain very hard.
The field got wet and muddy.
The coach moved the match to next Saturday.
Ana frowned and sat down.
Then she played a soccer video game with Ben at home.

passages.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
sentences: It was a hot, dry day, and a crow was very thirsty.
She flew down to a tall pitcher of water.
The water was low, at the very bottom of the pitcher.
Her beak was too short to reach it.
The crow looked around and saw some small stones.
She picked up one stone and dropped it into the pitcher.
The water rose a little bit.
She dropped in more stones, one by one.
Each stone pushed the water higher.
Finally, the water was near the top, and the crow drank it.

credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly

passages.title: Priya's Rover Stops
sentences: On Thursday, Priya took her rover to the park to test it on the grass.
She drove it in a big circle around a bench.
Then the rover slowed down and stopped in the middle of the path.
The little light on top had turned red.
Priya remembered that a red light means the battery is empty.
She had played with the rover all morning and forgot to charge it.
Priya carried the rover home and plugged it in.
After one hour, the light turned green, and the rover worked again.

passages.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
sentences: A hare liked to tell everyone that he was the fastest animal in the forest.
One day, a tortoise said, "Let's have a race."
The hare laughed, because he was sure he would win.
The animals marked a path from the big oak tree to the river.
When the race began, the hare ran so fast that he was soon far ahead.
He looked back and saw that the tortoise was far behind him.
"I have lots of time," thought the hare, so he lay down under a tree for a nap.
The hare fell asleep, and he slept for a long time.
Meanwhile, the tortoise walked slowly and steadily, one step at a time.
He passed the sleeping hare and kept going.
When the hare woke up, he ran as fast as he could.
But the tortoise had already crossed the finish line by the river.

credit.title: The Tortoise and the Hare
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Domino Run
sentences: On Friday after school, Leo and Maya built a domino run in the school library.
It had five hundred dominoes and went around two tables.
Mr. Hill said they could start it at four o'clock so the club could watch.
Ten minutes before four o'clock, a strong wind blew in through an open window.
It pushed a sheet of paper off a desk, and the paper slid into the last domino.
That domino hit the next one, and a long line fell backward.
Maya gasped, and Leo ran to the middle of the line.
He pulled out three dominoes to make a gap, and the line stopped falling at the gap.
Only fifty had fallen.
Maya closed the window, and they set the fallen ones up again.
At four o'clock, the club watched the whole run fall in a perfect line.

passages.title: Leo's Wet Socks
sentences: Leo skated home from the park.
Dark gray clouds filled the sky.
Soon, the streets were wet, and there were puddles everywhere.
Leo got home and took off his shoes.
His socks were very wet.
He put them by the heater to dry.

passages.title: The Empty Plate
sentences: Grandma Rose put a plate of ham sandwiches on the low table in the living room.
Then she went to the kitchen to make some tea.
Sam was upstairs, building a model train track.
Pixel stayed in the living room, next to the sandwiches.
Five minutes later, Grandma Rose came back with the tea.
The plate was empty, and there were crumbs on the rug.
Pixel was licking his nose and wagging his tail.
Sam was still upstairs with his train track.

passages.title: The Bird Bowl
sentences: On Friday evening, Ben filled a bowl with water for the birds.
He put it on the back step.
That night, the weather report said it would be very cold.
In the morning, Ben went out to check the bowl.
The water was hard and cold, and it stayed in the bowl when he tipped it.
A small bird landed on top of it and slid across.
Ben smiled and went inside to get some warm water.

passages.title: The Snapped Chain
sentences: On Saturday morning, Leo and Ben rode their bikes to the trails in Story Woods.
They planned to ride up to the old mill and eat lunch by the creek.
Halfway up the first hill, Ben's chain snapped with a loud click.
His pedals spun around, but the back wheel did not move.
Ben got off and looked at the broken chain lying in the dirt.
"Okay, let's think about what we can do," Leo said in a calm voice.
They could push both bikes up to the mill, but that was two more miles.
They could call Ben's dad, but he was at work until three o'clock.
Or they could walk back down to Okafor's Bike Shop, which was only ten minutes away.
They chose the bike shop.
Mr. Okafor fixed the chain with a new link while the boys waited.
Then they rode back up the hill and ate a late lunch by the creek.

passages.title: No Ferry Today
sentences: For three weeks, Ms. Ortiz's science class had been getting ready for a trip to Seal Point.
Seal Point is a rocky island across the bay, where dozens of seals rest in the sun.
The plan was to take the nine o'clock ferry, count the seals and record what each one was doing.
Sam had even drawn a map of the island that showed the best places to stand.
But on Tuesday morning, a strong wind was pushing tall, gray waves into the harbor.
When the class reached the dock, a sign on the ferry office said, "All ferries cancelled today because of high wind."
A few students groaned, and Sam slowly folded his map in half.
Ms. Ortiz read the sign twice, and then she turned to face the class.
"Our plan has changed, so let's look at our choices," she said in a calm voice.
She wrote three choices in her notebook and read them aloud.
The class could go back to school and watch a video about seals.
They could wait on the dock in case the wind dropped.
Or they could visit the Sea Center next to the ferry office, which has a touch tank full of crabs and sea stars.
Priya pointed to the word "today" on the sign and asked Ms. Ortiz to cross out waiting.
Ben said a video would be fine, but at the Sea Center they could study real animals.
The class voted, and most students chose the Sea Center.
Inside, they counted eleven crabs and seven sea stars, and Sam drew a new map that showed where each animal was hiding.
Before they walked back to school, Ms. Ortiz phoned the ferry company and moved the Seal Point trip to the next Tuesday.

passages.title: The Dough That Did Not Rise
sentences: Every Saturday, Rose's Bakery sells forty loaves of seed bread, and Sam helps Grandma Rose bake them.
On Friday evening, she mixes the dough and leaves it in big bowls so it can rise slowly overnight.
Dough rises because yeast, a tiny living thing in the dough, makes bubbles of gas when it is warm.
But this Saturday, when Sam lifted the towels off the bowls, the dough was just as flat as it had been the night before.
Grandma Rose did not panic.
"Let's check one thing at a time," she said.
First, Sam read the recipe card while Grandma Rose checked her notes from the night before, and every amount matched.
Next, they looked at the yeast packet, and its date showed that it was still fresh.
Then Sam noticed that his fingers felt cold, so he looked at the thermometer on the wall.
It showed only 48 degrees, which was much colder than the bakery usually was.
Grandma Rose checked the heater and found that it had switched off.
A storm had made the power go out for a short time in the night, and the heater had not turned back on.
Grandma Rose nodded, because now she knew why the dough was still flat.
She pressed the heater's reset button, and warm air began to blow.
Then she and Sam moved the bowls beside the warm oven and covered them with clean towels.
Sam made a sign for the door that said, "Fresh bread at 11 AM today. Thank you for waiting!"
By ten o'clock, the dough had doubled in size, and at eleven the first warm loaves were on the shelves.

credit.title: The Dough That Did Not Rise

passages.title: The Rained-Out Final
sentences: Ana and Ben's soccer team had won every game that autumn, and the league final was set for Saturday morning at the Harbor Middle School field.
Grandma Rose had promised to bring orange slices, and Sam had painted a banner for the fence.
But on Friday night, heavy rain began to fall, and it was still falling the next morning.
When the twins reached the field in their raincoats, wide puddles covered the center circle, and the grass squelched under their shoes.
Their coach was already there, talking with the groundskeeper, who looks after the school's grass.
A few minutes later, she told the team that the league did not allow games on a flooded field, so the final could not be played that day.
Ben stared at the puddles and let out a long breath, but he did not argue.
"We have a problem to solve," the coach said, "so let's look at every choice before we pick one."
Grandma Rose offered the back room of her bakery, just across the street, as a dry place to think.
There, the coach wrote four choices on a large sheet of paper.
The team could play in the school gym that afternoon, play on the field on Sunday, play on the following Saturday, or share the trophy with the other team without playing.
Next, they checked each choice carefully.
Ana phoned the school office and learned that a basketball tournament had booked the gym for the entire weekend.
Ben opened the weather map on his tablet, which showed rain until late Saturday night and then sunshine all day on Sunday.
However, the groundskeeper had explained that soaked grass needs two full dry days before it is firm enough for a game.
Sharing the trophy was still possible, but nobody on the team wanted to finish the season without playing the final.
Only one choice was left: the following Saturday.
Before anyone cheered, the coach phoned the other team's coach to make sure the new date worked for both teams, and he agreed.
The team spent the rest of the morning in the bakery, planning new plays and eating Grandma Rose's orange slices.
One week later, the final was played under a clear sky on a dry, firm field.

passages.title: The Upside-Down Map
sentences: Sam and Ben wanted to hike to the old mill in Story Woods.
Sam carried the trail map, and Pixel walked next to him.
At a fork in the trail, Sam looked at the map and turned left.
Twenty minutes later, the boys came to the creek, not the mill.
Sam looked at the map again.
The arrow for north was pointing down at his shoes.
He had held the map upside down, so he had turned the wrong way.
Sam turned the map the right way up.
Then the boys walked back to the fork and turned right.
Soon they saw the old mill in front of them.

passages.title: Clouds over Lantern Peaks
sentences: On Friday night, Sam, Maya and Grandma Rose drove up to the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
They wanted to watch a meteor shower.
Meteors are tiny bits of space dust and rock that burn up high in the sky and make bright streaks of light.
But when they got out of the car, thick clouds covered the whole sky.
They could not see a single star.
Maya sighed, and Sam stared up at the gray sky.
Then Grandma Rose said, "Our plan has changed, so let's think about what we can do."
They could wait in the car and hope the clouds would move.
They could drive home right away.
Or they could visit the observatory next to the lookout, which was open late.
They chose the observatory.
Inside, a guide showed them photos of meteors and said the shower would go on for three more nights.
Sam checked the weather report, and it said the sky would be clear on Saturday.
So on Saturday night, they drove back up and counted twenty-two meteors.

words.means: a building with big tools for looking at stars
a high place where you can see far
a time when many bits of space rock fall and glow

passages.title: The Silent Keyboard
sentences: Ben plays the keyboard in the Harbor Middle School jazz band.
On Wednesday night, he practiced a new song at home.
He wore headphones, so the music would not bother Ana while she did her homework.
When he finished, he packed the keyboard into its case.
He did not unplug the headphones, so they went into the case too.
The next day, the jazz band met in the music room to practice.
Ben switched on his keyboard, and the green power light came on.
But when he pressed the keys, the speakers made no sound at all.
Leo, who plays the drums, came over to help.
Leo saw a thin black cord going from the back of the keyboard into the case.
It led to Ben's headphones.
On his keyboard, when headphones are plugged in, the sound goes only to them and not to the speakers.
Ben unplugged the headphones and pressed a key, and a clear note rang out.
The jazz band started the new song on time.

passages.title: The Dull Agates
sentences: For a month, Maya had been polishing beach agates in a rock tumbler in Ms. Ortiz's classroom.
A rock tumbler is a small barrel that turns slowly, day and night, with stones, water and grit inside.
Grit is a sandy powder that grinds the stones smooth.
Every week, Maya washed the stones and the barrel, and then she added a finer grit.
In the last week, she used a polish that should make the agates bright and shiny.
But when Maya opened the barrel on Friday, the agates were dull and cloudy.
Under a magnifying glass, she could see tiny scratches all over them.
Ms. Ortiz explained that scratches like these usually come from coarse grit, the roughest kind, which Maya had used in the first week.
Together they searched the barrel and found a few coarse grains stuck in a narrow groove inside the lid.
Maya had scrubbed the barrel every week, but the groove was too thin to see into.
During polish week, the hidden grit had fallen out and scratched the stones as they turned.
The school rock show was fifteen days away, so Maya and Ms. Ortiz compared two fixes.
Maya could start over with coarse grit, which would take four more weeks.
Or she could scrub the lid groove with an old toothbrush and repeat only the fine grit and polish weeks.
Ms. Ortiz said the scratches were shallow enough for fine grit to remove them.
Maya chose the second fix, because it would take two weeks and be ready in time.
Two weeks later, the agates came out bright and smooth, and the next day Maya set twelve of them on a black cloth at the rock show.

passages.title: The Concert Moves Inside
sentences: The Grade 6 band at Harbor Middle School had practiced for six weeks for its summer concert.
The concert was planned for two o'clock on Saturday, at the bandstand in the harbor park.
Maya would play the flute, and Ana would play the trumpet.
On Saturday morning, a strong wind began to blow in from the sea.
Flags on the harbor flapped hard, and paper cups rolled across the park.
At the bandstand, the wind kept lifting the sheet music off the music stands.
Ms. Gray, the music teacher, gathered the band under the roof of the bandstand.
"The wind has changed our plan, so let's list what we could do," she said calmly.
The band could play outside and hold the music down with clothespins.
They could move the concert to the school gym, which was free all afternoon.
Or they could wait and play on the next Saturday.
Maya tried two clothespins on her stand, but the wind still bent the pages and turned them over.
Ana said that many families had already planned to come today.
So the band chose the gym.
Moving the concert caused a new problem, because the families would go to the harbor, not the school.
Sam drew a simple map from the bandstand to the gym, and Ms. Gray taped copies to the bandstand posts.
The school also sent a message to every family about the new place.
At two o'clock, almost every chair in the gym was full.
The band played all six songs, and not one page blew away.

passages.title: The Cracked Wheel
sentences: Every spring, the observatory on Lantern Peaks holds Mars Day, and the biggest event is the rover challenge.
Behind the observatory is the Mars yard, a field of red sand, gravel and rocks that looks like the surface of Mars.
Each rover must drive from the starting line to a flag and back, and the fastest rover that finishes wins.
Priya wanted her rover to be faster this year.
So she replaced its heavy rubber wheels with light plastic wheels that she had printed on the school's 3D printer.
An hour before the challenge, Priya and Sam took the rover for a practice run.
Halfway across the yard, it rolled over a strip of sharp gravel, and one plastic wheel cracked.
After that, the cracked wheel could not grip the ground, so the rover kept pulling to the left.
It drove in a slow circle and never reached the flag.
Priya carried the rover back to her table and took a long, slow breath.
"My plan has to change, but we still have an hour," she said.
Sam remembered reading that a real rover on Mars once got holes in its wheels from sharp rocks.
Its team on Earth kept driving it, but they planned routes that went around the sharpest rocks.
Priya could do the same thing: put on her one spare plastic wheel and steer around the gravel.
That plan was fast, but if a second wheel cracked, she would have no spare left.
Her other choice was to put the old rubber wheels back on.
They were heavy and would make the rover slower, but they had crossed sharp gravel many times without any damage.
Priya read the rules again, and they said that a rover that stops before the flag gets no score.
She decided that finishing was more important than being fast, so she chose the rubber wheels.
In the challenge, her rover rolled straight over the gravel, touched the flag and came back.
It finished in third place, and Priya wrote a new goal in her notebook: design a light wheel that is also strong.

passages.title: The Rained-Out Dig
sentences: Last summer, paleontologists from the Harbor Town Museum discovered the bones of a duck-billed dinosaur in Red Rock Quarry.
Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils, which are the remains or traces of living things from long ago, preserved in rock.
This kind of dinosaur ate plants and lived more than 66 million years ago.
The museum invited Ms. Ortiz's science club to help with the excavation, or careful digging, on the first Saturday in October.
Maya packed her own soft brush and a notebook for sketching every bone the club uncovered.
But heavy rain fell all Friday night and continued into Saturday morning.
When the club arrived, the lead paleontologist, Dr. Bell, was waiting for them at the museum instead of the quarry.
She explained that the rain had turned the clay in the quarry into deep, slippery mud.
In mud, diggers cannot tell where a bone ends and the surrounding rock begins, so they could easily damage a fossil by accident.
For that reason, her team never excavates in the quarry while the ground is wet.
Maya looked down at her brush and was quiet for a moment.
Then she asked Dr. Bell what the club could do instead.
Dr. Bell described two possible choices.
The club could go home and wait for a dry Saturday to dig.
Or they could spend the morning in the museum's preparation lab, where workers carefully clean bones that were collected last summer.
Ben worried that the lab would be boring, but Dr. Bell promised that the club would use real tools on real fossils.
After a short discussion, the club voted for the lab.
In the lab, each student used a small metal pick and a soft brush to remove rock from around a bone.
The work was slow, because one careless scrape could chip the fossil underneath.
Maya uncovered part of a tooth, and she sketched it in her notebook.
Two weeks later, on a dry, sunny Saturday, the club finally excavated in the quarry and found a rib bone.

passages.title: Pixel's Muddy Paws
sentences: It rained all morning.
Then the sun came out.
Sam let Pixel out into the yard.
Pixel ran to the garden and dug a big hole.
The dirt was wet and soft.
Then Pixel ran back into the house.
He left brown paw prints all over the kitchen floor.
Sam got a towel and wiped Pixel's paws.
Then he mopped the floor.

passages.title: The Flat Ball
sentences: Ben kicked his soccer ball hard.
It sailed over the fence.
It landed in the neighbor's rose bush.
A sharp thorn poked a small hole in the ball.
Air escaped through the hole.
Soon the ball was completely flat.
Ben could not kick it.
His dad fixed the hole with a ball repair kit.
Then Ben pumped air into the ball.
He kicked it again, and it bounced high.

passages.title: The Long Train
sentences: On Monday morning, Sam rode the bus to school.
The bus stopped at the rail crossing near the harbor.
Red lights flashed, and the gate came down.
A long freight train rolled slowly past.
Sam counted the cars, and there were ninety-two.
The bus had to wait for twelve minutes.
When the gate went up, the bus drove on.
It got to Harbor Middle School after the bell.
The driver gave each student a note for the office.
The note said that a train had made the bus late.

passages.title: The Missing Game Piece
sentences: Ana and Ben set up a board game on the floor.
Each player needs four pieces of one color.
Ben picked blue, but he found only three blue pieces.
One blue piece was missing.
The twins looked in the box and under the rug, but they did not find it.
Then Ana found a small blue button in the craft box.
"This can be your fourth piece," she said.
They played the whole game with the button.
Later, Ben opened the rule book and found the blue piece stuck between two pages.

passages.title: Ana's Sticky Valve
sentences: Ana plays the trumpet in the school band.
A trumpet has three valves that you press down with your fingers.
On Tuesday, Ana pressed the first valve, and it stayed down.
Her notes sounded wrong.
Ms. Gray, the music teacher, looked at the trumpet.
"This valve is dry," she said.
Ana had not put oil on her valves for two months.
Ms. Gray put three drops of valve oil on the valve.
Then the valve went up and down smoothly.
Now Ana oils her valves every Friday.

passages.title: The Melting Ice Cream
sentences: It was a hot, sunny afternoon in Harbor Town.
Maya bought a cone of mint ice cream at the Lighthouse Café.
On the way home, she saw a sparkly rock next to the path.
She knelt down to look at it with her magnifying glass.
She looked at it for a long time.
When she stood up, green drops were running down her hand.
The hot sun had melted her ice cream.
Maya laughed and licked the drips off the cone.
Next time, she will eat her ice cream before she looks at rocks.

passages.title: Too Bright for Stars
sentences: On Friday night, Sam lay on a blanket in his backyard to look at the stars.
He could see only five stars.
The porch light was on, and it was very bright.
Bright lights make it hard to see dim stars.
Sam asked his dad to switch off the porch light.
Then Sam waited in the dark for twenty minutes.
Human eyes need time to get used to darkness.
Slowly, Sam could see more and more stars.
Soon he counted more than one hundred.

passages.title: The Slippery Gripper
sentences: Priya's robotics club built a robot arm for the school science fair.
The arm had a gripper with two flat plastic fingers.
Its job was to pick up a tennis ball and drop it into a bucket.
On Monday, Priya tested the arm ten times.
The fingers closed around the ball each time, but the ball slipped out seven times.
Priya looked closely at the fingers.
They were smooth and shiny, so they could not hold the fuzzy ball tightly.
Sam, who was helping, said the motor could squeeze the fingers harder.
But Priya worried that a harder squeeze might crack the plastic fingers.
Instead, she wrapped a thick rubber band around each finger.
Rubber is soft and grippy, so it does not slide easily.
Priya tested the arm ten more times, and the ball slipped out only once.
At the science fair, the arm dropped every ball into the bucket.

passages.title: No Signal in Story Woods
sentences: On Sunday, Sam and Maya hiked in Story Woods with Pixel.
Sam followed the Fern Loop trail with a map app on his phone.
Deep in the forest, the map on the screen suddenly went blank.
A message said, "No signal."
The steep hills surrounding them were blocking the phone signal.
Maya stopped walking and looked around at the trees.
"The phone map is not working, so let's think about our choices," Sam said calmly.
They could walk all the way back the way they came.
They could wait and hope the signal came back.
Or they could use the paper trail map that Sam always keeps in his backpack.
They chose the paper map.
Sam found the creek on the map, and they could hear the creek on their left.
That told them where they were on the trail.
They followed the trail signs and got back to the parking lot before lunch.

passages.title: The Skate Park Is Closed
sentences: Leo planned to practice a new trick at the skate park on Saturday morning.
Ben was coming to film it with his tablet.
But when they got there, a metal fence stood around the ramps.
A sign on the fence said, "Closed for repairs until Monday."
Workers were filling cracks in the concrete with fresh cement.
Leo let out a long sigh.
Then he said, "Okay. What else can we do today?"
Ben listed three ideas.
They could go home and play video games.
They could come back on Monday after school.
Or they could go to the smooth, flat lot behind the library, where skating is allowed.
Leo's new trick did not need a ramp, so they chose the library lot.
Leo practiced for an hour, and Ben filmed him landing the trick twice.
On Monday, they went back to try the repaired ramps.

passages.title: No Eggs for Muffins
sentences: On Sunday morning, Sam and Grandma Rose wanted to bake oat muffins for a picnic.
The recipe needed two eggs.
But when Sam opened the fridge, the egg carton was empty.
The corner store was closed until noon, and the picnic started at eleven.
Grandma Rose stayed calm.
"Let's list what we can do," she said.
They could skip the muffins and bring apples instead.
They could make a different snack that did not need eggs.
Or they could use mashed banana in place of the eggs.
Grandma Rose said that half of a mashed banana can take the place of one egg in muffins.
Sam found one ripe banana in the fruit bowl, which was just enough.
They chose the banana, because the muffins would still be ready in time.
The muffins came out soft and sweet, with a little banana taste.
At the picnic, Ana asked for the recipe.

passages.title: The Echo in the Gym
sentences: The school band had to practice in the gym for a week while the music room was painted.
The gym has a high ceiling, hard walls and a shiny wooden floor.
When the band played, the sound bounced off the walls and came back as echoes.
The echoes mixed with the new notes, so the songs were hard to hear clearly.
Maya could not hear her own flute, and Ben missed the moment to start his part.
Ms. Gray explained that hard, flat surfaces bounce sound back, but soft things soak it up.
The band dragged the thick blue gym mats over and stood them up against the walls.
They also hung two old stage curtains over the railings of the bleachers.
Then they played the first song again.
This time, the echoes were much quieter, and each instrument sounded clear.
Maya could hear her flute, and Ben started his part at the right moment.

passages.title: The Frozen Game
sentences: Ana and Ben were playing their favorite racing game in the living room.
Their game console sat on the floor, and Ben's jacket was lying on top of it.
After an hour, the picture froze in the middle of a race.
The console felt very hot, and its fan was loud.
Then the console switched itself off.
Ana looked up the problem in the console's instruction booklet.
It said that the console has vents that let hot air out.
If the vents are covered, the console gets too hot and turns off to protect itself.
Ben's jacket had been covering the vents the whole time.
Ben hung up his jacket, and the twins moved the console to an open shelf.
They waited ten minutes for it to cool down.
When they switched it back on, it worked, and it did not freeze again.

words.means: a game machine that plugs into a screen
small holes or slots that let air out

passages.title: The Tipping Dinosaur
sentences: Maya and Sam were building a wooden model of a long-necked dinosaur.
The kit had forty flat wooden pieces that slot together.
They built the four legs and the body first.
Then they slotted the long neck onto the front of the body.
But every time they let go, the model tipped forward and fell on its nose.
Sam looked at the picture on the box.
In the picture, a long tail stuck out behind the body.
"The tail balances the heavy neck, and we left it out," Sam said.
The tail pieces were still in the bag.
Maya slotted the tail onto the back of the body.
Now the neck at the front and the tail at the back balanced each other.
The model stood on its four legs without tipping.
Maya read that real long-necked dinosaurs also had long tails that helped balance their heavy necks.

passages.title: The Gulls at the Harbor
sentences: On a sunny Saturday, Sam, Leo and Priya ate lunch on a bench by the harbor.
Leo unwrapped his sandwich and set it on the bench beside him.
A seagull swooped down, grabbed half of the sandwich and flew away.
Soon five more gulls landed on the railing and watched the friends' food.
Priya said that gulls learn quickly where people leave food, so they keep coming back.
The friends talked about what to do.
Waving the gulls away would work for only a minute.
So they moved to a picnic table in the covered shelter by the ferry dock.
They kept their food in their lunch boxes and took out one piece at a time.
Now the gulls could not see any food, and they could not swoop under the roof.
After a few minutes, the gulls flew off to look somewhere else.
Sam gave Leo half of his own sandwich.

passages.title: Maya's Mixed-Up Labels
sentences: Maya keeps her rock and mineral collection in an egg carton with twelve cups.
She used to tape a small paper label with the rock's name onto each rock.
But tape does not stick well to rough, dusty rocks.
One day, Maya bumped the carton, and the rocks rolled across her desk.
Half of the labels fell off.
Now Maya could not remember which gray rock was granite and which was basalt.
At the rock club, Mr. Varga showed her how to tell them apart.
Granite has light and dark speckles, but basalt is dark gray all over.
Then he showed her a better way to label rocks.
Maya painted a small white dot on each rock and wrote a number on the dot.
In her notebook, she wrote each number next to the rock's name.
Now, even if the rocks spill, every rock still has its number.

passages.title: Rails in the Heat
sentences: Train tracks are made of long steel rails.
Like most metals, steel grows a tiny bit longer when it gets hot, and it shrinks again when it cools.
On a very hot summer afternoon, a rail in full sunshine can become much hotter than the air around it.
If a hot rail grows longer but has no room to move, it pushes sideways and can bend out of line.
Railway workers call this a "sun kink," and trains must slow down or stop until it is repaired.
Long ago, railways solved this problem by leaving small gaps between short rails.
Each gap gave the steel room to grow on hot days.
But the gaps caused new problems.
The wheels banged over every gap, which made the ride bumpy and wore out the wheels and the rail ends faster.
Today, many railways weld their rails together into one long, smooth rail with no gaps.
Before workers clamp the welded rail down, they warm it or stretch it, so it already has the length it would have on a warm day.
That way, it has much less need to grow when summer comes.
On the hottest days, some railways also paint the sides of rails white, because white reflects sunlight and keeps the steel cooler.
Trains may also run more slowly on very hot afternoons as an extra safety step.

words.means: to join metal by melting the ends into one piece
a sharp bend in something that should be straight

passages.title: Plaster Jackets for Fossils
sentences: Dinosaur bones that have been buried for millions of years are often cracked and fragile.
When paleontologists find one, the rock around it may be the only thing holding the pieces together.
If they lifted a large bone straight out of the ground, it could break into hundreds of pieces before it reached the museum.
To solve this problem, field teams build a hard case called a plaster jacket.
First, they dig a trench around the bone, so that it sits on a pillar of rock.
Next, they cover the bone with damp paper towels, so the plaster will not stick to the fossil.
Then they dip strips of rough cloth called burlap in wet plaster and lay them over the bone, one strip at a time.
When the plaster dries, it holds the bone still, the same way a cast holds a broken arm still.
Later, the team digs under the pillar, flips the whole block over and covers the bottom with plaster, too.
Large jackets can weigh as much as a car, so teams sometimes need a crane or a truck to move them.
At the museum, workers called preparators cut the jacket open with a small saw.
Then they spend months removing rock from the bone with tiny picks and soft brushes.

passages.title: The Sunny Corner
sentences: For the spring robot show, Priya's robotics club built a small robot that follows a line.
The track was a loop of black tape on the pale floor of the school library.
Under the robot's front edge, a light sensor shines a tiny beam at the floor and measures how much light bounces back.
The pale floor bounces back a lot of light, and the black tape bounces back very little, so the robot can tell where the line is.
All morning, the robot followed the line perfectly.
But at two o'clock, it rolled off the tape at the same corner three times in a row.
Priya noticed that the corner was beside a tall window, and bright afternoon sunlight now covered that part of the floor.
She guessed that the sunlight was shining into the sensor, so the black tape looked bright, too.
To test her guess, Leo held up a large book to block the sun, and the robot followed the line around the corner.
The club compared two fixes.
They could close the window blinds, which would take only a minute.
But Mrs. Hall, the librarian, explained that closed blinds would make the reading corner too dark for the students reading there.
The other fix was to build a small hood around the sensor to keep outside light away from it.
A hood would take longer to make, but it would work in any room at any time of day.
The club chose the hood, and Priya made it from black cardboard and tape.
After that, the robot followed the line through the sunny corner every time.

passages.title: Beehive Fences
sentences: In parts of Africa, elephants sometimes walk into farms at night and eat the crops.
A small group of them can eat or trample a whole field of corn in one night.
Farmers need their crops to feed their families, but most of them also want the elephants to stay safe.
Scientists noticed something useful: elephants stay away from bees.
A bee sting on the soft skin inside a trunk hurts.
So when elephants hear buzzing bees, they usually walk away.
The scientists helped farmers build beehive fences.
Hives hang from a wire that runs between wooden posts, with a hive about every ten meters around the field.
If an elephant pushes the wire, the hives swing, and bees fly out buzzing.
Most elephants then turn around and leave the crops alone.
In tests, the fences kept most elephants out of the fields.
The fences also helped farmers in a second way, because they could collect and sell the honey.
The bees also carry pollen from flower to flower, which helps nearby crops grow.
But the fences have limits: the bees need flowers and water nearby, and the hives must be checked often.

passages.title: Ice from the Lake
sentences: Before electric refrigerators, keeping food cold in summer was a hard problem.
Milk turned sour, butter melted, and meat spoiled quickly in the heat.
Tiny living things called bacteria grow fast in warm food, but cold slows them down.
Many towns solved the problem with winter ice.
When lakes froze thick in January, workers cut the ice into large blocks with long saws.
Horses pulled the blocks to an ice house, a building with thick walls and almost no windows.
Inside, workers packed sawdust around every block.
Sawdust holds lots of trapped air, and trapped air slows heat from moving into the ice.
Packed this way, much of the ice stayed frozen until autumn.
In summer, an ice wagon delivered blocks to homes, and families kept them in a wooden icebox.
The ice sat in the top part of the icebox, and cold air sank down over the food below.
As the ice melted, the water dripped into a pan that someone had to empty every day.
If people forgot, the pan overflowed onto the kitchen floor.

words.means: went bad and was not safe to eat
tiny bits of wood made when wood is cut

passages.title: Water on the Space Station
sentences: The International Space Station is a science lab that circles Earth about 400 kilometers above the ground.
The crew on board needs water to drink, to cook, to wash and to grow plants.
But water is heavy, and sending it up on a rocket costs a lot of money.
Each supply rocket can carry only so much, and it must also bring food and tools.
Engineers solved this problem by making the station clean and reuse almost all of its water.
When astronauts breathe and sweat, they put tiny amounts of water into the air.
Machines cool the station's air.
Then the water in the air forms drops, like the drops on a cold glass on a hot day.
The machines also collect used wash water and the crew's urine.
Then they filter and clean all of this water until it is purer than most tap water on Earth.
Today, the station reuses about 98 out of every 100 liters of its water.
The system does need care, though, because filters fill up and parts sometimes break.
So the crew keeps spare parts on board, and supply rockets still bring a small amount of fresh water.

passages.title: The Cancelled Train
sentences: For a month, Sam had been counting the days until his trip to the Pine Bay Train Museum.
Grandma Rose had bought two tickets for the 9:10 AM train, and the museum's old steam engine would run at eleven o'clock.
Sam had even marked the route on his map: fifty-five minutes along the coast, over three bridges and through one tunnel.
But when they reached the Harbor Town station, the screen above the platform said, "9:10 to Pine Bay: CANCELLED."
A station worker explained that a signal on the line had stopped working, so no trains could pass until it was repaired.
Sam stared at the screen, and his face felt hot.
He took a slow breath and asked Grandma Rose, "What are our choices?"
Together they found three.
They could ride the replacement bus, which would leave at 9:30 and reach Pine Bay at 10:45.
They could wait at the station for the signal to be fixed, but the worker did not know how long that would take.
Or they could go home and use their tickets on another Saturday.
Sam checked the times again and saw that the bus would still get them to the museum before eleven o'clock.
The bus was not a train, but it followed the coast road, and Sam could see the railway line from his window most of the way.
They walked into the museum at 10:50, just in time to watch the steam engine roll out of its shed.
By the evening, the signal had been repaired, so they took the train home instead of the bus.

passages.title: Pixel and the Fence
sentences: Every afternoon that week, Pixel dug a hole under the back fence and squeezed into the neighbor's yard.
Each time, the neighbor kindly walked him back to Sam's front door.
Sam wanted to stop the digging, but first he wanted to understand why it was happening.
He noticed that Pixel dug only on long school days, when nobody had taken him for a walk.
Sam's dad said that many dogs dig when they have extra energy and nothing to do.
Sam and his dad talked about two fixes.
One fix was to bury chicken wire along the bottom of the fence, so Pixel could not dig through.
The other fix was to give Pixel more exercise and a place where he was allowed to dig.
The wire was quicker, so they tried it first.
The wire stopped the digging, but it caused a new problem.
With nothing to do, Pixel began barking at the fence for an hour at a time.
So Sam added the second fix, too.
Each morning, he walked Pixel for thirty minutes before school.
He also built a sandbox in a corner of the yard and buried a chew toy in it.
Pixel spent his afternoons digging up the toy, and the barking stopped.

passages.title: Two Groups, One Gym
sentences: On rainy days, the twins' soccer team practices in the Harbor Middle School gym.
One wet Wednesday, Ana and Ben arrived with their teammates at five o'clock, ready to run drills.
But the gym was already full of tables, because the chess club was holding its yearly tournament there.
The school calendar showed both groups in the gym at the same time, because two bookings had been typed into the same time slot by mistake.
Coach Novak looked at the rows of chess boards and nodded slowly.
"Two groups and one gym," she said, "so let's work this out together."
She and the chess teacher listed three choices.
The team could practice in the covered area by the bus stop, which was dry but small.
The two groups could share the gym, but bouncing balls would distract the chess players.
Or the team could skip practice today and practice twice next week.
Ben pointed out that the covered area was too small for running drills but big enough for passing drills in pairs.
Ana added that passing was the skill the team most needed to practice before Saturday's game.
So the team practiced passing under the roof for one hour.
Afterward, some players tiptoed into the gym to watch the last round of the tournament.
Coach Novak and the chess teacher also asked the office to add a check so that one room cannot be booked twice.

passages.title: Game Night in the Dark
sentences: Every Friday, Ana and Ben host a game night for their friends.
This Friday, Leo, Maya, Sam and Priya came over to play a new racing game on the big screen.
Halfway through the first race, the lights flickered, and then the whole house went dark.
The screen went black, and the game stopped.
Ben's mom found a flashlight and checked her phone.
A message from the power company said that a fallen branch had cut the power on their street.
The power would be back in about two hours.
Leo groaned, and then he laughed.
"We need a new plan," Ana said, "so let's list what we can do without power."
They could play the racing game on Ben's tablet, but its battery was low, and only two people could play at a time.
They could play a board game by flashlight.
Or they could end game night early and go home.
Priya pointed out that a board game would let all six friends play at once and would not need any power.
Maya found four flashlights and stood them on the shelves, pointing up at the white ceiling, so the light spread over the whole table.
They played a game about building train lines across a map, and Sam won by two points.
At nine o'clock, the lights came back on, but by then nobody wanted to stop the board game.

passages.title: The Flooded Trail
sentences: Last spring, a family of beavers moved into the creek that runs through Story Woods.
Beavers build dams out of branches, mud and stones to create deep ponds, where they can swim safely and store branches to eat in winter.
Within a month, the new dam had raised the water so much that the pond spread across the trail beside the creek.
Hikers had to turn back, and the trail crew worried that the soaked ground would wash away.
A park ranger explained the problem to Ms. Ortiz's science club during a visit.
Simply tearing out the dam would not work, because beavers usually rebuild a broken dam within a few days.
Moving the beavers to another place was possible, but the pond had become a home for frogs, ducks and herons, and those animals would lose it too.
The ranger wanted a solution that would keep the beavers and also keep the trail dry.
The answer came from a surprising fact about how beavers behave.
Beavers repair a dam when they hear or feel water rushing through it.
So the trail crew pushed a long plastic pipe through the dam, with its far end lying deep in the pond, several meters upstream.
They put a wire cage around that end, so the beavers could not block it with sticks.
Now water flows quietly into the deep end of the pipe and out below the dam, and the beavers cannot hear the leak.
The pond dropped about half a meter, which was enough to uncover the trail.
The fix did cause one small new problem.
Leaves and twigs sometimes collect on the cage, so the crew must clear it every few weeks.
The club agreed that a few minutes of cleaning was worth it for a dry trail and a pond full of wildlife.

passages.title: Glasses for a Space Telescope
sentences: In 1990, scientists launched a large telescope into orbit around Earth.
High above the air, which blurs starlight, it was supposed to take the sharpest pictures of space ever made.
But when the first pictures came back, the stars looked fuzzy, with a soft glow around each one.
Engineers studied the pictures and found the cause: the telescope's main mirror had been ground to the wrong shape.
The mistake was tiny, only about one-fiftieth of the width of a human hair, but a telescope mirror must be almost perfect, so it was enough to blur every image.
The mirror was 2.4 meters wide and built deep inside the telescope, so it could not be replaced in space.
Bringing the whole telescope back to Earth would have been extremely difficult and expensive.
Then the engineers realized something useful.
Because they could measure exactly how wrong the mirror was, they could design new parts with the opposite error.
Light would bounce off the faulty mirror, pass through the new parts and come out focused, the same way glasses help a person see clearly.
In December 1993, a team of astronauts flew up to the telescope on a space shuttle.
During five spacewalks, they installed a set of small correcting mirrors and a new camera that had the correction built in.
When the next pictures arrived, the stars were sharp points of light.
The fix did cause a small new problem: the correcting mirrors took up space, so the astronauts had to remove one science instrument to make room.
Later missions built the correction into every new instrument, so the extra mirrors were removed in 2009.
The telescope is still working today, more than thirty years after it was launched.

words.means: a path that goes around and around Earth

passages.title: Stuck in the Sand on Mars
sentences: In 2004, two robot rovers landed on Mars to study its rocks and soil.
Each rover was about the size of a golf cart and was driven by a team of engineers on Earth.
Radio signals take several minutes to travel between Earth and Mars, so the drivers could not steer the rovers live, the way a player steers a car in a video game.
Instead, they sent a list of commands each day, and the rover carried them out by itself.
In April 2005, one rover, named Opportunity, was driving across a field of sand ripples, which are low waves of sand shaped by the wind.
It tried to cross a ripple that was softer than it looked, and its six wheels dug deep into the loose sand.
The wheels kept spinning, but the rover barely moved.
If the team simply sent more "drive forward" commands, the wheels might dig even deeper and trap the rover for the rest of the mission.
So the team did not rush.
On Earth, engineers built a copy of the ripple in a test area, using a soft mix of sand and clay that behaved like the Mars sand, and they buried a test rover in it the same way.
For weeks, they tried different ways of driving the test rover out, and they measured which moves worked best.
Then they sent Opportunity commands to drive a few centimeters at a time, and they checked the results after each small move.
After about five weeks, in early June 2005, Opportunity rolled free.
Getting stuck also taught the team a lesson for the rest of the mission.
They studied photos of the ground more carefully, and they planned routes that went around soft ripples.
The safer routes meant the rover took longer to reach new places, but it kept exploring Mars until 2018.

passages.title: Water in the Mine
sentences: On a class trip to the Ridgeway Mine Museum, Mr. Varga led the students down a long, sloping tunnel into the old mine.
Halfway down, he stopped beside a rusty iron pipe as thick as a tree trunk.
"Listen," he said, and the students heard a steady drip somewhere in the dark.
He explained that rainwater soaks down through soil and cracks in the rock, so water slowly gathers in the deepest tunnels of a mine.
Hundreds of years ago, as miners dug deeper, many mines filled with water faster than workers could carry it out in buckets.
At first, miners used pumps turned by horses walking in circles or by water wheels on nearby streams.
These pumps helped, but they could not lift water from very deep tunnels, and a strong stream was not always nearby.
In the early 1700s, inventors built some of the first useful steam engines to solve exactly this problem.
A fire boiled water to make steam, and the steam helped rock a huge wooden beam up and down, which worked a pump far below.
Steam pumps were strong enough to drain much deeper mines, and they could be built anywhere, even far from a stream.
Steam pumps solved the flooding, but they caused new problems of their own.
They burned huge amounts of coal, which cost a lot of money and filled the air with smoke.
For the next hundred years, engineers worked to build engines that did the same work with less fuel.
Maya asked how the museum keeps its own tunnels dry today.
Mr. Varga pointed to a small gray box on the wall: an electric pump with a float switch.
When the water at the bottom rises, a float lifts and switches the pump on, and when the water drops, the pump switches itself off.
"It is the same problem with a much smaller machine," he said, and the class followed him deeper into the mine.

passages.title: Bridges and the Wind
sentences: A long bridge must hold up its own weight, the cars and trucks that cross it, and a force that nobody can see: the wind.
When wind blows across a bridge, it pushes on the deck, which is the flat road part that vehicles drive on.
Engineers have learned that wind can do more than push.
As air flows over and under a flat, solid deck, it can form swirls that tug the deck up and down, again and again.
If those tugs match the natural rhythm of the bridge, the bouncing can grow larger, the way a swing goes higher when you push it at just the right moment.
To prevent this, engineers test a bridge design before they build it.
They make a small, exact model of the bridge and place it in a wind tunnel, a long tube where powerful fans blow air at different speeds.
Sensors on the model measure every movement, so the engineers can find problems while the bridge is still a model.
When a test shows too much movement, engineers can change the shape of the deck.
Some modern decks are shaped like a flat box with sloped edges, so the air slides smoothly past without forming strong swirls.
Other bridges use open frames of steel beams called trusses, which let much of the wind pass straight through.
Some very long bridges even have a gap down the middle of the deck so air can flow between the two halves.
Each fix has a cost.
A deep steel truss is heavy and needs more metal, which makes the bridge more expensive to build and to paint.
A deck with a gap must be wider to fit the same number of lanes.
So engineers compare the choices and pick the shape that stays steady in the wind and is also sensible to build.

passages.title: Harbor Town's Flood Plan
sentences: Mill Creek flows out of Story Woods and runs through the low part of Harbor Town before it reaches the harbor.
For years, heavy spring rain made the creek overflow its banks, and water flooded the streets near the library and the bus station.
Shops had to close, buses took long detours, and families spent days cleaning mud out of their basements.
The first step in the town's plan was a flood map.
After each storm, workers marked which streets had water and how deep it was.
They shaded the map from light blue for shallow water to dark blue for deep water.
The finished map showed something surprising: the worst flooding always started at one narrow bend near the old bridge.
There, the creek squeezed through a small pipe under the road.
The town council then compared two fixes.
The first fix was to build tall concrete walls along both banks of the creek.
Walls would keep water off the nearby streets, but an engineer warned that the water would rush faster between them and could flood the farms farther downstream.
The second fix was to replace the small pipe with a wide bridge and to turn an empty field beside the creek into a park that is allowed to flood.
During a big storm, extra water would spread across the park's low grass and soak in slowly, instead of rushing into town.
The council chose the second fix, partly because the park would also give the town a new place for soccer and picnics on dry days.
The park caused one small problem of its own: after each flood, a layer of mud and branches is left on the grass.
Now volunteers hold a cleanup morning after big storms, and the soccer field is usually ready again within a week.
Since the park opened three years ago, the streets near the library have not flooded once.

words.means: the land along the sides of a creek
a group of people chosen to run the town
farther along, the way the water flows

passages.title: Finding the Way at Sea
sentences: For hundreds of years, sailors on long ocean voyages faced a serious map problem.
To mark a ship's position on a map, a navigator needed two numbers.
Latitude tells how far north or south a ship is, and longitude tells how far east or west it is.
Latitude was fairly easy to find, because sailors could measure how high the sun was at noon or how high the North Star was at night.
Longitude was much harder, and a ship that guessed it wrong could sail right past the island it was looking for.
The answer came from a surprising place: a clock.
Earth turns once every 24 hours, so each hour of difference in time equals 15 degrees of longitude.
If a navigator knew the exact time back at the home port and the time on the ship, the difference showed how far east or west the ship had sailed.
Time on the ship was easy to find, because the sun is highest in the sky at noon.
The hard part was keeping the home port's time.
The best clocks of that time used swinging pendulums, which did not work on a rolling ship.
In the 1700s, one clockmaker spent decades building clocks that could keep accurate time at sea.
Instead of a pendulum, his clocks used springs and balanced wheels, and they adjusted for heat and cold.
On a test voyage across the Atlantic Ocean in 1761, his best clock lost only about five seconds.
The new sea clocks were very expensive at first, so only some ships carried them.
Over the next hundred years, makers learned to build them more cheaply, and most ocean ships carried at least one.
Today, ships find their position with signals from satellites, and those satellites also depend on extremely exact clocks.

passages.title: Coral Gardens
sentences: Coral reefs look like colorful rocks under the sea, but they are built by tiny animals called coral polyps.
Each polyp builds a hard cup of limestone around its soft body.
Over many years, millions of these cups join together to form a reef.
Reefs give food and shelter to about one quarter of all kinds of ocean animals, even though they cover less than one percent of the ocean floor.
In many places, reefs have been damaged by storms, by water that is too warm and by boat anchors dropped on them.
Many corals grow only a few centimeters a year, so a damaged reef can take decades to grow back by itself.
Scientists and divers found a way to help, called coral gardening.
First, divers collect small broken pieces of healthy coral, which can keep growing if they are given a safe place.
They hang the pieces on frames shaped like trees, made of plastic pipes and fishing line, a few meters below the surface.
This underwater garden is called a nursery.
Hanging in open water, the pieces get plenty of light and moving water, and they are safe from sand and from animals that eat coral.
In a nursery, some corals grow much faster than they would on the reef floor.
After six months to a year, divers carry the grown pieces back to the damaged reef.
They attach each piece to the rock with a small dab of underwater cement or a plastic tie.
Over time, the pieces grow together, and fish return to the reef.
Coral gardening has limits.
It is slow, careful work, and divers can plant only a small area each year compared with the huge size of the world's reefs.
It also cannot help if the water stays too warm, so scientists say it is even more important to protect healthy reefs before they are damaged.

passages.title: The Flat Tire on Lantern Peaks
sentences: Ms. Ortiz's class had waited all term for their visit to the observatory on Lantern Peaks.
Dr. Lee, the scientist who runs the big telescope, had planned a morning with two parts: a tour of the telescope dome at ten o'clock and a sun-watching session at eleven.
For the sun session, she would use a special telescope with a filter, because looking at the sun is safe only through the right kind of filter.
But halfway up the winding road, the bus driver heard a thumping sound and pulled into a wide parking area.
One of the back tires was flat, so the bus could not go any farther.
A few students groaned, and Leo leaned his forehead against the window.
Ms. Ortiz phoned Dr. Lee, explained the problem and then turned to the class.
"We have a new problem to solve, so let's look at every choice," she said.
A spare bus could come from town, but it would not arrive until almost eleven o'clock.
The class could walk the rest of the way, but the road had no sidewalk and climbed steeply for two more kilometers.
Or they could ride the spare bus back to school and book another visit, but Dr. Lee's calendar was full until spring.
Priya pointed out that waiting for the spare bus meant missing the dome tour but still reaching the sun session.
Then Dr. Lee offered to give the dome tour by video call, so the class could watch it on Ms. Ortiz's tablet while they waited.
Everyone agreed that this plan saved the most of their morning.
The spare bus arrived at five minutes to eleven, and the class reached the observatory just as the sun session began.
Through the filtered telescope, Sam counted four dark sunspots, and Maya sketched each one in her notebook.
Before they left, Dr. Lee invited the class to see the real dome in person at the spring open house.

passages.title: The New Cello String
sentences: An hour before the winter concert, Priya opened her cello case in the music room and began tuning her strings.
As she tightened the peg for the highest string, there was a sharp snap, and the string curled up, loose and useless.
The string had been on the cello for two years, and Ms. Gray explained that old strings gradually wear thin and can break under tension.
Priya had an important solo in the second piece, and almost every note of it was played on that string.
Priya held the broken string and closed her eyes for a moment.
Then she and Ms. Gray calmly listed the possible choices.
Ms. Gray had a replacement string, but a brand-new string keeps stretching for a day or two, so it gradually slides out of tune.
The school also owned an extra cello that was already tuned, but it was a smaller size, so Priya's fingers would land in slightly different positions.
A third possibility was to let Ben play the solo melody on the piano, although Priya had practiced it for six weeks.
Priya tested a few notes on the smaller cello and missed two of them.
So she chose the replacement string, and Ms. Gray helped her attach it.
To deal with the stretching, Priya tuned the new string and gently pulled it away from the fingerboard several times.
Pulling helps a new string stretch faster, so afterward she tuned it again.
She also asked Ms. Gray for a short pause between the first and second pieces, so she could check her tuning once more.
During the first piece, the new string slipped slightly flat, which means a little too low, exactly as Ms. Gray had predicted.
Priya used the pause to adjust it, and her solo in the second piece sounded clear and steady.
Afterward, she wrote a reminder in her practice notebook: "Replace old strings a week before a concert, not an hour before."

passages.title: The Sign That Turned
sentences: On Saturday morning, Sam and his dog Pixel set off on the trail to the old mill in Story Woods.
Sam had walked there twice before, but always with Grandma Rose, who remembered every turn.
This time, he planned to follow the wooden trail signs on his own.
At a fork in the path, a sign with the words OLD MILL pointed to the left.
Sam turned left, and Pixel trotted ahead with his nose close to the ground.
Twenty minutes later, the path ended at the creek, and Sam could not see the mill anywhere.
Sam stopped and took the paper map out of his backpack.
On the map, the trail to the mill went right at the fork, not left.
He also remembered that a powerful wind had swept through the forest the night before.
Sam and Pixel walked back to the fork to look at the sign more closely.
The sign hung on a single bolt, and the bolt was loose.
When Sam touched the sign, it swung around easily on its post.
The wind had spun it, so the arrow pointed the wrong way.
Sam took the trail to the right and reached the mill fifteen minutes later.
At the ranger hut, he told Ranger Cole about the loose sign.
The next day, Ranger Cole fixed the sign with two new bolts so it could not turn.

passages.title: The Seals Slide Away
sentences: Leo had saved his birthday money for a camera with a long zoom lens.
On Saturday, he took the 9:00 ferry to Gull Island to take photos of the seals.
His cousin Max, who is seven, came with Leo and his mom.
When they reached the seal beach, about twenty seals were lying on the flat rocks near the water.
Leo set up his camera at the top of the beach.
Before he could take a single photo, a family with a beach ball walked down toward the rocks to get a closer look.
One seal lifted its head and barked.
Then, one by one, all the seals slid off the rocks and into the sea.
A ranger walked over and explained that seals rest on land to warm up and save energy.
When people come close, the seals do not feel safe, so they escape into the water.
The ranger showed everyone a wooden platform on the hill above the beach.
From there, visitors could watch the seals without being seen.
Leo, Max and Leo's mom climbed up and waited quietly for half an hour.
Slowly, the seals came back and pulled themselves onto the rocks.
With his zoom lens, Leo took a clear photo of a young seal yawning.

passages.title: The Kite That Spun
sentences: Ben had built a new kite for Kite Day at Windy Cape, and he had tested it in the park in Harbor Town.
In the park, the wind was gentle, and the kite flew smoothly with its short tail.
On the cliff top at Windy Cape, the wind was much stronger.
As soon as Ben let go, the kite shot up, spun in a circle and dove into the grass.
He tried three more times, and each time it spun and fell.
Ben sat down on the grass, and Ana sat down next to him.
Captain Ada, a pilot who also flies kites, walked over to look.
She explained that a kite's tail pulls on the bottom of the kite and keeps its nose pointed into the wind.
In a gentle wind, a short tail is enough.
In a strong wind, the kite twists much harder, so it needs a longer tail to stay steady.
Ana had a roll of ribbon in her bag.
Ben tied on three more meters of ribbon, so the tail was much longer than before.
This time, the kite climbed high above the cliffs and stayed there, pointing straight into the wind.
Captain Ada said that pilots also change their plans when the wind changes.

passages.title: The Flat Battery
sentences: On Wednesday afternoon, Captain Ada climbed into the Kookaburra to start its engine for the first time in months.
She turned the key, but nothing happened.
The engine made no sound, and the lights on the panel stayed dark.
Mr. Lund came over from his workbench with a small meter in his hand.
He tested the plane's battery and shook his head.
"The battery is flat," he said. "There is no power left in it."
Captain Ada thought back to the afternoon before.
She had sat in the cockpit for an hour, testing the lights and the radio.
To make them work, she had turned on the master switch, which sends power from the battery to everything in the plane.
When she finished, she climbed out and closed the door.
She had forgotten to turn the master switch off, so power slowly drained out of the battery during the night.
Mr. Lund connected the battery to a charger, and they waited three hours while it filled with power again.
Then Captain Ada turned the key, and the engine started with a steady hum.
Afterward, she added a new line to the end of her checklist: "Turn the master switch OFF before you leave the plane."
"Now the list will remind me," she said.

passages.title: Fog at Cloud Hill
sentences: Captain Ada had planned to take off from Cloud Hill at eight o'clock on Monday morning.
But when she opened the hangar doors at seven, she could not see the end of the runway.
Thick white fog covered the whole airfield.
A pilot in a small plane like the Kookaburra must be able to see where she is going.
So the Kookaburra could not leave in the fog.
Mr. Lund came into the hangar with two cups of tea and looked out at the fog.
"Last night was clear, cold and very still," he said.
He explained that on a night like that, the ground loses its heat and becomes cold.
The air just above the ground cools down too.
Cold air cannot hold as much water as warm air, so some of the water turns into tiny drops.
Millions of those tiny drops floating near the ground are what we call fog.
Captain Ada did not like waiting, but she knew that morning fog often goes away when the sun warms the air.
She phoned the island where she planned to stop for fuel and said she would be two hours late.
Then she and Mr. Lund checked the map together while the sun climbed higher.
By ten o'clock, the fog was gone, and the runway was bright and clear.

passages.title: Why Kip Would Not Eat
sentences: One Tuesday morning, Ranger Tess noticed that Kip had not touched his breakfast.
The fresh branches in his yard were still covered with leaves.
Kip sat high in his tree, sniffing the air, and did not climb down to eat.
Ranger Tess checked him carefully, and he looked healthy and bright.
So she knew that something was wrong with the leaves, not with Kip.
Ranger Tess thought back to the day before.
That day, the road to the usual forest had been closed for repairs.
Because of that, Ranger Owen had cut leaves from a different group of trees beside the river.
Those trees were eucalyptus trees too, but they were a different kind.
There are hundreds of kinds of eucalyptus, and each koala eats only a few of them.
Kip had smelled the leaves and decided they were not his food.
Ranger Tess phoned Mr. Jamison, a farmer who has the right kind of eucalyptus trees along his fence.
He said she could cut as many branches as she needed.
By noon, fresh branches from the farm were in Kip's yard.
Kip climbed down right away and began to eat, one leaf at a time.
That afternoon, Ranger Tess wrote a list of the right trees for each koala, so this would not happen again.

passages.title: The Moon Without Shadows
sentences: Leo wanted a sharp photo of the Moon's craters for his science project.
On a Friday night, he went to the observatory at Star Point with his mom.
The Moon was full, round and very bright, and the sky had no clouds at all.
Dr. Amal pointed the big telescope at the Moon and checked that it was in focus.
Leo held his phone camera up to the eyepiece and took ten photos.
At home, Leo looked at the photos on his computer.
The edge of the Moon was sharp, but the middle looked flat and pale.
He could hardly see a single crater.
The next day, he sent the photos to Dr. Amal and asked what had gone wrong.
Dr. Amal wrote back that nothing was wrong with his phone or the telescope.
When the Moon is full, the Sun shines straight onto the side we see.
The craters have almost no shadows, so their shapes are hard to see.
When only half of the Moon is lit, the sunlight comes from the side.
Then each crater has a dark shadow, and it stands out clearly.
Leo checked a Moon calendar and came back three weeks later, on an evening with a half Moon.
This time, his photos showed hundreds of round craters along the line between light and dark.

passages.title: The Train That Did Not Stop
sentences: Maya collects striped pebbles, and she had read that the beach at Shell Halt is full of them.
On Sunday, she bought a ticket from Pier Station to Shell Halt and took the 11:30 Coast Line train.
She sat by the window with an empty cloth bag on her lap.
After ten minutes, she saw the small Shell Halt sign beside the track.
Maya was surprised when the train did not slow down.
It rolled past the empty platform and kept going along the coast.
Maya walked to the conductor and asked why the train had not stopped.
The conductor explained that Shell Halt is a request stop.
At a request stop, the train only stops if a passenger tells the conductor before the stop.
If people are waiting on the platform, they raise a hand so the driver can see them.
Nobody had asked, and nobody was waiting, so the driver did not stop.
At Rail Coast, Maya looked at the timetable by the ticket window.
The next train back toward Pier Station left at 12:40.
As soon as she got on, she told the conductor that she wanted to get off at Shell Halt.
This time, the train slowed down and stopped at the little platform.
Maya filled half her bag with striped pebbles before the 2:15 train came by.
When she saw it coming, she raised her hand, and the driver stopped for her.

passages.title: Sam's Bag of Shells
sentences: Sam had read that Fossil Bay was one of the best places on the coast to find fossils.
On the boat from Gull Island, he told Dr. Bell that he hoped to find a dinosaur bone.
After three hours of searching the beach, his bag was heavy, but it held only shells.
There were coiled ammonites, tiny clams and small pointed fossils called belemnites, all made of gray stone.
Sam showed his bag to Dr. Bell and asked why he could not find any dinosaurs.
Dr. Bell pointed up at the gray cliff with its thin layers of rock.
She explained that millions of years ago, this whole place was under a warm, shallow sea.
Ammonites and other sea animals lived in that sea, and when they died, their shells sank to the sea floor.
Mud settled over the shells, layer after layer, and over a very long time the mud was pressed into rock.
Slowly, the shells inside the rock turned into fossils.
Dinosaurs lived on land, so only a few of their bones ever reached the sea floor.
Over millions of years, the land rose, and the old sea floor became the cliff.
Every winter, waves and rain wear away a little of the cliff, and new fossils fall onto the beach.
Sam looked at his heavy bag again.
He decided that a bag full of sea animals from the time of the dinosaurs was a very good find.

passages.title: The Broken Coral
sentences: Mari has driven the reef boat at Reef Island for nine years.
When she started, every boat that stopped in the lagoon dropped an anchor.
An anchor is a heavy hook on a chain that holds a boat in one place.
On sand, an anchor does no harm.
But in the lagoon, many anchors landed on coral.
Over time, Mari noticed broken pieces of coral near the places where boats often stopped.
When a boat swung in the wind, its anchor chain dragged across the reef and snapped off more branches.
This was a big problem, because coral grows very slowly.
Some kinds grow only about one centimeter in a whole year, so a broken patch can take many years to grow back.
Mari met with the island helpers to find a way to protect the coral.
Together, they set six heavy blocks on the sandy floor of the lagoon, away from the coral.
A rope runs from each block up to a bright float on top of the water.
Now boats tie up to a float instead of dropping an anchor.
Last week, Priya helped Mari tie the boat to one of the floats.
Through the glass floor, she saw small new branches of coral growing near the old broken pieces.
